situation: You are the one who keeps proposing plans with a friend. Time together is lovely, but when you stop texting, contact stops too. What you know is the pattern of who initiates; what you do not know is why, whether your friend would welcome the conversation, and whether the imbalance bothers you enough to raise it.

minds.title: The Plain Speaker
minds.concern: Say what is true early and kindly, before quiet resentment does the talking.
minds.author: Marshall Rosenberg

minds.title: The Story Auditor
minds.concern: Separate what you observed from the story your mind builds around it.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

minds.title: The Maintenance Realist
minds.concern: Friendships need upkeep, and the upkeep is rarely split evenly.
minds.author: Robin Dunbar
minds.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Say something, and soon. If you keep texting while keeping score privately, resentment grows where your friend cannot see it. A short, warm message about what you have noticed and what you would like costs little. Silence lets her assume you are perfectly happy with the pattern.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Story Auditor
debate.text: Slow down. What you actually know is that you start the plans and that nothing arrives when you stop. Why is a story your mind is eager to write: she does not care. We judge from the evidence in front of us and ignore what is missing. What might be missing here?
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Quite a lot. Friendships fade without contact, and someone has to supply it. Often one person simply becomes the organizer. The lovely meetups suggest the bond works. So I would test it: stop texting for a month and let the pattern become information rather than a guess.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: That is a test your friend does not know she is taking. If she fails, you learn little, since she may just be waiting for a cue. If she passes, she may be confused about the sudden silence. Honest beats clever. Name what you notice, how it feels, and what you would like.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Story Auditor
debate.text: Fair, secret tests are slippery, and I concede that. But look at your own sentence, Plain Speaker: nothing happens is a count of one channel, the texts. Does she ever send a link, a photo, a reply that opens a thread? Keep the claim narrow until you have checked.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: I would go further than Dunbar here, and this is my own extension. Some people are warm in person but poor at logistics, and an unprompted text feels to them like an interruption. That is a guess, not his finding. It does show one behavior can have very different causes, so phrasing matters.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Which is exactly why speaking beats guessing. But I will revise: no accusations like you never reach out. Open with an observation, then a feeling, then a request she can actually say yes to. Rosenberg would call a sentence with a hidden verdict in it a disguised judgment.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Story Auditor
debate.text: Then my worry moves to the request. Ask her to initiate more and you may get a dutiful text she resents, a performance rather than interest. Ask for nothing and you stay where you are. So which do you want from this: equal effort, or simply to know where you stand?
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Those are different goals, and the answer changes everything. Many good friendships are lopsided by temperament, and carrying more of the load can be a fair price for something lovely. If the imbalance genuinely stings, naming it is justified. If it mostly does not, doing nothing is a legitimate choice.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Even a lopsided friendship may be worth one light remark, so she knows the effort exists. I concede it need not be a formal talk. A casual line over coffee, saying you would love it if she picked the next plan, honors both the friendship and the feeling.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Story Auditor
debate.text: In person, where the evidence is richest, I can accept that. Ask her what she would like plans to look like. My remaining objection is firm, though: do not walk in believing she does not care. That part is still unverified, and it would color every word you say.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

clearer: The main insight is that the question may be less whether to say something than what you want the conversation to find out: whether the friendship works for you as it is, or whether the imbalance is costing you more than the meetups give back. Still disputed is whether a quiet-month test is a useful experiment or an unfair trap, and how much a sting alone justifies speaking. A possible self-reflection: when you imagine her reply, which story are you already assuming, and what do you actually have evidence for?
dependsOn: If the imbalance stings or you notice yourself keeping score, a light, specific, non-accusing remark in person becomes more reasonable, because unspoken resentment can change the friendship anyway. If you mostly enjoy the friendship and the effort feels like a fair price, continuing as you are, or simply initiating a bit less, becomes more reasonable, because lopsided effort is common and not always a sign of low regard. If the decisive unknown is why she rarely initiates, a proportionate way to learn it is to look for other signs of interest she shows, and to ask her openly what she would like plans to look like, rather than going silent to see what happens.
